content: Caspase recruitment domains (CARDs) are specific protein interaction motifs that are commonly found in proteins involved in inflammation and apoptosis. These domains facilitate the assembly of larger protein complexes through direct interactions between individual CARDs. CARD domains are present in a diverse range of proteins, including helicases, kinases, mitochondrial proteins, caspases, and other cytoplasmic factors. CARD domains belong to a subclass of protein motifs known as the death fold. This structural motif is characterized by six to seven antiparallel alpha helices arranged around a hydrophobic core, with an outer surface composed of charged residues. Other motifs within this class include the pyrin domain (PYD), death domain (DD), and death effector domain (DED), all of which primarily function in the regulation of apoptosis and inflammatory responses. CARD domains were initially identified for their role in regulating caspase activation and apoptosis. The six-helix structure of the CARD domain is evolutionarily conserved, dating back to the ced-3 and ced-4 genes in Caenorhabditis elegans, where key components of the apoptotic machinery were first characterized. In mammals, CARD motifs are found in several proteins that promote apoptosis, including caspases 1, 4, 5, 9, and 15. In the mammalian immune response, CARD proteins play a critical role in regulating inflammation in response to bacterial and viral pathogens, as well as endogenous stress signals. For example, the NLR protein Ipaf-1 contains an N-terminal CARD domain, a nucleotide-binding domain, and C-terminal leucine-rich repeats (LRRs), which are thought to function similarly to those in Toll-like receptors. Ipaf-1 regulates the proteolytic processing of pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their mature forms by forming a large protein complex known as the inflammasome. Upon activation by intracellular bacteria such as Salmonella typhimurium or other stress signals, Ipaf-1 recruits a CARD-containing adapter protein called ASC and caspase-1 through CARD-CARD interactions. This complex leads to the autoprocessing and activation of caspase-1, which subsequently drives the maturation of IL-1β and IL-18. CARD proteins are also involved in antiviral signaling. A subset of CARD proteins, such as RIG-I and MDA5, recognizes intracellular double-stranded RNA, a common feature of many viral genomes, including those of paramyxoviruses, orthomyxoviruses, and rhabdoviruses. These proteins contain twin N-terminal CARD domains and C-terminal RNA helicase domains, which directly interact with and process double-stranded viral RNA. This processing exposes the CARD domains for interaction with the CARD motif of IPS-1/MAVS/VISA/Cardif, a downstream adapter protein anchored in the mitochondria. While in vitro studies have demonstrated interactions between IPS-1 and RIG-I/MDA5, the precise nature of the complex formed during viral detection remains unclear. Due to their role as regulators of inflammation, constitutive activation of certain CARD proteins—either through mutations or persistent stress signals—has been implicated in various inflammatory syndromes. For instance, gain-of-function mutations in the intracellular NOD2 protein have been associated with an increased risk of Crohn's disease. Similarly, activating mutations in two related PYD-containing proteins, cryopyrin/CIAS-1 and pyrin/MEFV, have been linked to Muckle-Wells Syndrome and familial Mediterranean fever, respectively.
